Effects of nano-bubble water on anaerobic co-digestion of cabbage waste and 
cow manure under mesophilic and thermophilic conditions
Youfei Zhoua, Peilin Guob, Yi Liub,c, Weijie Hua and Tianfeng Wangb
aDesign Institute No.3, Shanghai Municipal Engineering Design and Research Institute (Group) Co., Ltd., Shanghai, People’s Republic of China; 
bCollege of Petrochemical Engineering, Lanzhou University of Technology, Lanzhou, People’s Republic of China; cSchool of Environmental and 
Municipal Engineering, Xi’an University of Architecture and Technology, Xi’an, People’s Republic of China
ABSTRACT  
The impact of four nano-bubble water (NBW) additions on the hydrolysis rate, methane yield, and 
microbial community of co-digestion of cabbage waste (CW) and cow manure (CM) under 
mesophilic and thermophilic conditions were investigated. Adding NBW under mesophilic 
conditions promoted hydrolysis, and the highest soluble chemical oxygen demand of the 
mesophilic digesters with the addition of CO2-NBW increased by 15.86%. Methane yield in the 
mesophilic digesters with Air-NBW and CO2-NBW increased by 17.54% and 14.72%, respectively. 
Moreover, the addition of NBW further accelerated the methane yield rate under mesophilic 
conditions. Due to the influence of thermophilic temperature, the impact of NBW addition on 
hydrolysis, methane yield, and methane yield rate in the thermophilic digesters did not differ 
significantly from the control. The addition of Air-NBW and N2-NBW in the thermophilic 
digesters resulted in only marginal increases in methane yield, by 1.09% and 5.61%, 
respectively. NBW addition enhanced both the abundance and diversity of microbial 
communities in both mesophilic and thermophilic digesters. The addition of NBW represents a 
promising technological advancement for enhancing the efficiency of anaerobic co-digestion of 
CW and CM.

1. Introduction
As a predominantly agricultural nation, China generates 
an estimated 360 million tons of vegetable waste 
annually [1]. Cabbage waste (CW), a common food 
waste in China, is characterized by its high biodegrad­
ability [2]. Improper management of CW may result in 
significant health and environmental risks [3]. Anaerobic 
digestion (AD) offers an effective solution for treating 
CW by decomposing the organic matter in vegetables 
to produce biogas, while the resulting digestate serves 
as a valuable fertilizer [4]. The high volatile solids (VS) 
content (approximately 75%) and low total solids (TS) 
content (below 10%) in CW can lead to the accumulation 
of volatile fatty acids (VFA), which in turn may inhibit 
methanogenic activity and potentially result in the 
failure of the AD [3].
Co-digestion of CW and cow manure (CM) presents a 
promising strategy for stabilizing the AD process and 
enhancing methane yield [5]. Integrating CW and CM 
can effectively balance the water content, biodegrad­
able organic matter, and buffering capacity within the 
AD [3]. Vegetable peels were combined with CM under 
mesophilic anaerobic co-digestion conditions, achieving 
a methane yield of 170 mL g−1-VSadded [6]. However,

when the proportion of CW in the co-digestion was too 
high, the alkalinity of CM was not sufficient to buffer the 
hydrolysis to produce VFA, leading to the VFA accumu­
lation [3]. In response to VFA accumulation, the appli­
cation of additives, pH adjustments, or biofortification 
techniques can effectively mitigate acid inhibition [7]. 
Application of additives is an effective way to optimize 
the stability of CW and CM co-digestion systems and 
improve methane yield.
Adding biochar, zeolite, powdered activated carbon, 
and NaOH improved the stability of AD and increased 
methane yield [8]. Nano-bubble technology not only 
enhances the stability of AD and methane yield but 
also facilitates better utilization of the digestate, owing 
to the absence of chemical additives [9]. Nano-bubble 
water (NBW) is characterized by an abundance of 
nano-sized bubbles, which exhibit superior mobility 
and gas solubility than distilled water (DW) [10]. 
During their collapse, nano-bubbles generate substan­
tial amounts of reactive oxygen species, which in turn 
facilitate the hydrolysis of organic compounds [11,12]. 
NBW addition increased the activity of bacteria and 
methanogens, thereby promoting methane yield [13]. 
Air-NBW and O2-NBW enhanced the activity of faculta­
tive bacteria by creating a microaerobic environment, 
which in turn increased the efficiency of the electron 
transport system, thereby reducing the accumulation 
of VFA [14,15]. At the same time, NBW was added to 
increase alkalinity, improving buffering capacity and 
enhancing the stability of AD [9].
The addition of CO2-NBW into swine manure AD at 
8% TS effectively reduced the accumulation of VFAs, 
resulting in a cumulative methane yield of 261 mL 
g−1-VSadded [13]. The addition of N2-NBW and O2-NBW 
enriched the microbial communities and enhanced 
enzyme activity in the AD of corn straw, leading to 
increases in methane yield by 18.1% and 46.8%, respect­
ively [15]. The addition of N2-NBW to the AD of sludge 
increased methane yield by 29.0% compared with the 
control, the reason for which was mainly attributed to 
the enhancement of the enzyme activity of extracellular 
hydrolases by the addition of N2-NBW [16]. CW is easily 
hydrolyzed and acidified, CM is difficult to hydrolysis but 
can 
improve 
buffering 
capacity [3,6]. 
Achieving 
enhanced methane yield from AD necessitates a close 
linkage between the hydrolysis and methanogenesis 
stages, rendering the use of NBW to augment these 
stages a promising approach. The effect of NBW 
addition on the hydrolysis and methanogenic stability 
of CW and CM co-digestion is not known. Meanwhile, 
the effect of NBW addition on the changes of microbial 
communities during the co-digestion of CW and CM is 
also unclear.
In this study, the effect of adding four types NBW (Air, 
CO2, He, and N2) to the co-digestion system on the per­
formance of anaerobic co-digestion of CW and CM, and 
microbial community under mesophilic or thermophilic 
conditions was investigated. Enhancing a deeper under­
standing of NBW’s role in the co-digestion of CW and CM 
is crucial for optimizing its application in co-digestion 
systems.
2. Materials and methods
2.1 Batch anaerobic fermentation experiments
2.1.1 Raw materials and inoculum
The CW was sourced from a wholesale vegetable market 
located near the laboratory in Lanzhou, China. The CM 
was sourced from a dairy farm on the outskirts of 
Lanzhou, where predominantly Chinese Holstein cows 
are bred. Prior to the experiment, the CW was crushed 
using a grinder and homogenized to prepare it as fer­
mentation material, after which it was stored together 
with the CM in a refrigerator at 4 ± 1 °C for preservation. 
The inoculum used in the mesophilic and thermophilic 
digesters consisted of mesophilic and thermophilic 
seed sludge, which had been pre-adapted in the labora­
tory. The major characteristics of the various substrates 
utilized in this study are summarized in Table 1.
2.1.2 Production of NBW
The production of NBW with different gases was carried 
out using a nano-bubble water generator (JXWNP-AL01, 
Jinxiang, China). The NBW generated by this instrument 
featured an average nano-bubble particle size of 135.8 
nm and a concentration of 537 million nano-bubbles 
mL−1 (Figure S1). Gas (Air, CO2, He and N2) was vented 
into distilled water through the generator for 20 
minutes at 20 ± 2°C, followed by a 10 min stand period 
to obtain the NBW. During the NBW preparation 
process, the inlet pressure was maintained between

0.4 and 0.5 MPa. After production, NBW was quickly

2.1.3 Experimental setup
Based on previous research finding, a CW-to-CM ratio of 
1:1 on a wet basis has been shown to higher methane 
yield [3]. Consequently, the CW and CM were mixed in 
a 1:1 ratio on a wet basis. The mixed substrate was 
mixed with an equal mass of either NBW or DW, resulting 
in a total mass of 1500 g. The five experimental groups in 
the experiment were DW, Air-NBW, CO2-NBW, He-NBW, 
and N2-NBW were added, respectively. These five exper­
imental groups underwent batch AD experiments under 
thermophilic or mesophilic conditions. Under mesophi­
lic conditions, five groups were designated as M, M-Air, 
M-CO2, M-He, and M-N2. Under thermophilic conditions, 
the five groups were designated as T, T-Air, T-CO2, T-He, 
and T-N2. Subsequently, 500 g of mesophilic or thermo­
philic seed sludge was added to the corresponding 
digesters.
The entire digestion process was conducted in a 
digester with a working volume of 2 L. The digester 
was sealed with a specialized lid designed for AD, 
through which two metal tubes with an internal diam­
eter of 4 mm were inserted. Metal tubes with silicone 
tubing at both ends were employed for sampling via 
peristaltic pumps, while metal tubes with silicone 
tubing extending outside the bottle were used to 
connect to gas bags for biogas collection. The entire 
experiment was temperature controlled using a water 
bath, maintaining the mesophilic digesters at 37 ± 1 °C 
and the thermophilic digesters at 55 ± 1 °C. Each 
morning, each digester was manually shaken for 1 min. 
All digesters were run in triplicate.
Following the scheduled shaking of the digester, a 
peristaltic pump was used to withdraw a portion of 
the digestate mixture. The mixture was then centrifuged 
at 2000g for 5 min, after which the supernatant was 
filtered through a 0.45-μm polyether sulphone microfi­
bre filter. The resulting filtrate was utilized for sub­
sequent experimental analyses. A 5 g sample of the 
mixed digestate was taken at a predetermined time as 
the microbiological sample, and stored at −80 °C until 
sequencing.
2.2 Analytical methods
TS, VS, pH, soluble chemical oxygen demand (SCOD), 
total ammonia nitrogen (TAN), and total alkalinity (TA) 
were analysed following the standard methods [17]. 
Free ammonia nitrogen (FAN) was calculated based on 
pH, TAN, and temperature [18]. VFA was quantified 
using a gas chromatograph (SP-7890 Plus, Ruihong, 
China) equipped with an organic acid analytical 
column (320 µm inner diameter, 0.50 µm film, and 30 
m total length) and a flame ionization detector. The 
biogas volume was measured using an acid gas flow 
metre (LML-2, Alpha, China), while the methane concen­
tration was assessed using a biogas composition analy­
ser (GA5000, Geotech, United Kingdom).
Deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) was extracted from the 
digestate at specific intervals, followed by microbial 
abundance and diversity analysis using high-throughput 
sequencing to assess differences in microbial commu­
nities across co-digesters treated with different types 
of NBW under different temperature conditions. The 
V3-V4 hypervariable regions of the bacterial 16S rRNA 
gene were amplified using the primers 341F (5’- 
CCTACGGGNGGCWGCAG-3’) 
and 
806R 
(5′-GGAC­
TACHVGGGTATCTAAT-3′). The 
V4-V5 
hypervariable 
regions of the archaeal 16S rDNA gene were amplified 
using the primers Arch519F (5′-CAGCMGCCGCGGTAA- 
3′) and Arch915R (5′-GTGCTCCCCCGCCAATTCCT-3′). In 
brief, DNA was extracted from each digestate sample 
using the HiPure Soil DNA Kit (Magen, Guangzhou, 
China), followed by sequencing on the Illumina MiSeq 
platform (AxyPrep DNA Gel Extraction Kit, Axygen Bio­
sciences, Union City, CA, U.S.). The raw microbial sequen­
cing data were deposited in NCBI (https://www.ncbi.nlm. 
nih.gov/), with accession numbers PRJNA1043753 for 
bacteria and PRJNA1043758 for archaea.
2.3 Statistical analysis
Data analysis was performed using SPSS for Windows, 
version 22.0. Differences between experimental groups 
were evaluated using analysis of variance (ANOVA), 
with a significance level set at p < 0.05. Spearman corre­
lation analysis was conducted to examine the relation­
ship 
between 
the 
microbial 
community 
and 
environmental factors. The Modified Gompertz model 
was applied to fit the methane yield data.
3. Results and discussion
3.1 Characteristics of the digestate
The pH is an essential indicator of AD, with an optimal 
range for methanogenic activity being 6.5–8.0; devi­
ations from this range can adversely affect methanogen 
performance [19]. Under mesophilic conditions, the pH 
initially decreased, then increased during the initial 
stage of AD, and ultimately stabilized between 7.5 and 
7.7 (Figure 1a). Under thermophilic conditions, pH 
increased during the initial stage and eventually stabil­
ized between 8.0 and 8.1 (Figure 1b). The enhanced

hydrolytic capacity under thermophilic conditions in AD 
releases more ammonia nitrogen, while the accelerated 
reaction rate leads to faster VFA consumption, resulting 
in a higher pH under thermophilic conditions compared 
with mesophilic conditions [3]. The addition of CO2-NBW 
lowered the pH of both mesophilic and thermophilic 
digesters. The pH was similar to that of the CW and 
CM co-digestion systems with NaHCO3 addition, but 
the digestate from AD with NBW addition was more 
advantageous for land use [3].
SCOD reflects the quantity of organic matter in diges­
ters and the processes by which microorganisms 
produce or consume SCOD in AD [20]. Under mesophilic 
conditions, SCOD increased rapidly due to hydrolysis 
and subsequently decreased as methane production 
progressed (Figure 1c). Under thermophilic conditions, 
SCOD decreased continuously throughout the digestion 
process (Figure 1d). After day 28, all digesters reached a 
steady state in terms of SCOD due to the depletion of 
organic matter, with no significant differences observed 
among the digesters at this stage. At the end of AD, 
SCOD remained at a certain concentration, likely due 
to the presence of non-bioavailable organic matter, 
such as humic acids, within the digester [21]. Through­
out AD, SCOD in all digesters were lower than those 
reported in previous study [3]. This reduction could be 
attributed to the addition of NBW or distilled water 
(DW), which likely enhanced mass transfer efficiency 
and improved organic matter utilization, as well as to 
the dilution effect [22,23].
Ammonia is typically produced through the hydroly­
sis of proteins in the substrate, TAN and FAN were higher 
under thermophilic conditions than under mesophilic 
ones [3] (Figure 1e–h). This is primarily due to the 
enhanced hydrolytic capacity under thermophilic con­
ditions [9]. During AD, both TAN and FAN exhibited an 
increasing trend; however, methanogenic activity was 
inhibited when TAN levels exceeded 1500 mg L−1 or 
FAN levels exceeded 250 mg L−1 [3,9]. But ammonia inhi­
bition in AD is typically influenced by multiple factors 
[24]. Based on the trend of SCOD, ammonia nitrogen 
in digesters did not negatively impact methane pro­
duction, nor was there evidence of acid accumulation. 
TAN was greater but FAN was lower compared with pre­
vious study [3]. This suggests that NBW promoted the 
activity of hydrolysis enzymes to release more 
ammonia nitrogen, while lowering the pH to alleviate 
the inhibition of FAN to improve the stability of the 
system.
VFA are produced during the hydrolysis-acidification 
stage and consumed during the methanogenesis 
stage, serving as crucial intermediate products in the 
AD process [3,19]. Consequently, VFA initially increased 
and then decreased in the digesters (Figure 2). Under 
mesophilic conditions, VFA initially increased and then 
decreased. In the initial stage of mesophilic digestion, 
acetic acid predominated, while in the later stage, pro­
pionic acid became the dominant VFA. This shift is 
closely related to the Gibbs free energy of the various 
VFAs and the lower hydrogen partial pressure required

for the degradation of propionic acid [21]. The VFA of the 
digesters with added NBW was higher than that of the 
digesters with added DW, suggesting that NBW can 
promote hydrolysis and acidification [25]. On day 7, 
the butyric acid in the digesters with Air-NBW was 
lower than in the other digesters. Under thermophilic 
conditions, VFA increased and then decreased, with 
minimal variation after day 14. The rates of VFA pro­
duction and consumption in the thermophilic digesters 
were higher than those in the mesophilic digesters, con­
sistent with previous study [3]. The high temperature 
enhanced the hydrolysis of AD and the dissolution of 
organic matter, which increased the digestion rate of 
AD [9]. The VFA trends in mesophilic and thermophilic 
digesters were consistent with previous study, but the 
concentrations observed during AD were notably 
higher in both mesophilic and thermophilic digesters 
[3]. This increase may be attributed to differences in 
the AD substrate characteristics and the addition of 
NBW, which enhances hydrolysis [13].
TA (Figure 3a,b) serves as an indicator of the buffering 
capacity of the AD system, which is mainly provided by 
ammonia nitrogen [8]. The TA trends indicated no signifi­
cant differences among the experimental groups across 
varying temperatures when different types of NBW 
were added. The TA was lower than the results of the pre­
vious study, but the previous study added NaHCO3 [3]. 
The ratio of total volatile fatty acids to TA (TVFA/TA) 
(Figure 3c,d) is used to assess the stability of AD, with 
values exceeding 0.4 generally indicating instability 
[3,6]. In all digesters, TVFA/TA initially increased and 
then decreased, reflecting the production of VFAs 
during hydrolysis and acidification and their subsequent 
consumption during methanogenesis. In contrast, the 
thermophilic TVFA/TA was lower than that of the meso­
philic digesters and stabilized more quickly. This is attrib­
uted to the faster reaction rates under thermophilic 
conditions, which led to more rapid VFA consumption 
[3]. The TVFA/TA for Air-NBW under mesophilic con­
ditions was lower than that of the other groups during 
the mid-stage of digestion, indicating that Air-NBW 
enhanced VFA consumption and improved system stab­
ility [9,23]. The TVFA/TA ratio in the thermophilic diges­
ters with NBW was not significantly different from that 
of the control digesters, possibly because the thermophi­
lic predominantly influences hydrolysis, thereby dimin­
ishing the additional effects of NBW [26,27].
3.2 Methane yield
A modified Gompertz model was employed to fit the 
cumulative methane yield (CMY) (Figure 4
and 
Table 2). The fitting results showed a satisfactory agree­
ment with the experimental results (R2 ≥ 0.9936). Under 
mesophilic or thermophilic conditions, the methane 
content of biogas did not differ significantly between 
experimental groups, ranging from 56.06% to 58.34%. 
Compared with thermophilic conditions, the addition 
of NBW significantly enhanced methane yield under 
mesophilic conditions.
Under mesophilic conditions, the ultimate methane 
yield (UMY) was obtained in the digesters added with

231.23 (M-CO2) > 218.24 (M-He) > 201.56 (M) > 178.84 
(M-N2) mL g−1-VSadded, M-Air, M-CO2 and M-He were 
17.54%, 14.72% and 8.28% higher than M, respectively. 
The methane yield of M-Air and M-CO2 was significantly 
(p < 0.05) increased compared with M. The addition of 
iron filings to the co-digestion of barley and swine 
manure has been shown to enhance methane yield by 
8.7% to 28.6% [28]. Similarly, the addition of cow 
manure-based biochar in mesophilic AD resulted in a 
32.2% increase in methane yield [29]. However, the pro­
duction of biochar and the addition of iron filings con­
tribute to increased treatment costs and pose 
limitations for land application. The addition of Air- 
NBW facilitates the creation of a micro-oxygen environ­
ment during the hydrolysis stage of AD [30]. This 
environment enhances the activity of hydrolytic and 
acidogenic bacteria, thereby promoting the degradation 
of organic matter, which ultimately results in M-Air 
achieving the highest UMY [14]. The addition of CO2- 
NBW also contributed to an increase in UMY under 
mesophilic conditions, likely due to the addition of 
CO2, which enhanced the activity of hydrogenotrophic 
methanogens and bolstered system stability [25].
The addition of Air-NBW and CO2-NBW significantly 
enhanced methane yield in the mesophilic digesters. 
However, previous study reported methane yield 
increases of 20.8% and 19.1%, respectively, which are 
higher than the gains observed in this experiment [23]. 
This discrepancy may be due to the high cellulose 
content in the CM, which likely impeded hydrolysis 
[23]. The addition of NBW mitigated the sharp drop in 
pH by acting as a buffer, accelerating the production 
and consumption of reducing sugars and VFA, and the 
addition of NBW simultaneously enhances the microbial 
activity of the rich microorganisms contained in the CM 
and promoted methane yield [22,31].
Under thermophilic conditions, the UMY was 
obtained in the digestors added with NBW following a 
descending order: 276.89 (T-N2) > 265.03 (T-Air) >  
262.18 (T) > 245.67 (T-CO2) > 215.51 (T-He) mL g−1-

were 5.61% and 1.09% higher than T, respectively. The

The rate of methane yield in the mesophilic diges­
ters (Figure 4c) initially increased and then declined, 
peaking on day 21. The mesophilic digesters added 
with NBW exhibited higher initial rate of methane 
yield. This finding aligns with previous research indi­
cating that NBW supplementation enhances the rate 
of methane yield [23,30]. Under thermophilic con­
ditions, the rate of methane yield (Figure 4d) also 
rose initially and then declined. In contrast to the 
mesophilic 
digesters, 
the 
thermophilic 
digesters 
achieved its maximum methane yield on day 7 and 
day 14, which occurred earlier than in the mesophilic 
digesters. Compared with mesophilic conditions, ther­
mophilic conditions enhanced the solubility of organic 
matter, accelerated both biological and chemical pro­
cesses, and reduced the retention time [3]. The fitting 
results indicated that the mesophilic digesters with 
Air-NBW and CO2-NBW additions had a shorter lag 
phase, and the thermophilic digesters with Air-NBW 
had an even shorter lag phase. The lag phase in the 
thermophilic digesters were significantly shorter com­
pared with the mesophilic digesters. This confirms that 
higher temperatures accelerate biological and chemi­
cal reaction rates [3].
3.3 Dominant microbial community
3.3.1 Alpha diversity in bacteria and archaea
Observed species (sobs) represent the number of 
detected OTUs, with larger values indicating higher 
diversity. A higher Chao1 value reflects greater microbial 
diversity in the digesters [3]. Both the sobs and Chao1 for 
bacteria in the mesophilic and thermophilic digesters 
with NBW addition were higher than those in the 
control group (Table S1), suggesting that NBW enhances 
bacterial diversity in the digesters. Simpson and 
Shannon, on the other hand, reflect the microbial diver­
sity in the samples [25]. Therefore, the bacterial abun­
dance in the mesophilic and thermophilic digesters 
with NBW addition was higher compared with the 
control. In terms of alpha diversity for archaea (Table 
S2), the Chao1 in the mesophilic digesters with He- 
NBW and N2-NBW additions were lower than those in 
the control, indicating reduced archaeal diversity com­
pared with the control group. The archaeal diversity in 
the thermophilic digesters with Air-NBW were lower 
than in the control. However, based on the Shannon 
and Simpson, both mesophilic and thermophilic diges­
ters with NBW exhibited greater archaeal diversity com­
pared with the control. A previous study reported that 
digesters with Air-NBW and CO2-NBW additions had 
higher OTUs and Chao1 for both bacteria and archaea 
[32].
3.3.2 Dominant bacterial community
Under mesophilic conditions, the bacterial community 
was predominantly dominated by Firmicutes and Bacter­
oidota on both day 6 and day 28 (Figure 5). Firmicutes 
and Bacteroidota are capable of degrading organic 
matter into VFA, H2 and CO2, which are utilized by 
methanogens [33]. Additionally, Firmicutes serve as indi­
cators of AD stability. Firmicutes exhibited a significant 
negative correlation with TA (p < 0.01, R = −0.7118), pro­
pionic acid (p < 0.001, R = −0.8838), and butyric acid (p  
< 0.01, R = −0.6874) (Figure S2). The addition of Air- 
NBW and He-NBW increased the relative abundance 
(RA) of Bacteroidota under mesophilic conditions. Bacter­
oidota exhibited a higher RA in digesters with the 
addition of NBW [32]. Bacteroidota demonstrated a sig­
nificant positive correlation with TA (p < 0.001, R =  
0.7665) and propionic acid (p < 0.001, R = 0.7856). Pro­
teobacteria are capable of metabolizing complex 
organic matter to produce acetic acid [34]. The higher 
RA of both Proteobacteria and Bacteroidota suggests 
that the digestion of acetic acid, leading to methane 
yield, is more likely to occur in the digesters [34]. The 
RA of Proteobacteria appeared to decrease as digestion 
progressed. The addition of Air-NBW, He-NBW, and 
CO2-NBW to the mesophilic digesters effectively 
increased the RA of Proteobacteria. Proteobacteria exhib­
ited a significant positive correlation with UMY (p < 0.01, 
R = 0.7092).
Under thermophilic conditions, the bacterial commu­
nity was predominantly dominated by Firmicutes on 
both day 6 and day 28 (Figure 5). The thermophilic 
digesters with different NBW amendments exhibited 
greater bacterial abundance on day 6 compared with 
those with DW. The addition of NBW enriched Thermoto­
gota during the initial stage of AD (day 6). A decline in 
the RA of Thermotogota was observed in the later 
phase of AD (day 28) within the He-NBW and N2-NBW 
amended digesters. Thermotogota is a thermophilic bac­
terium responsible for fibre degradation and VFA pro­
duction in thermophilic digesters [35]. Thermotogota 
exhibited a significant negative correlation with TAN 
(p < 0.01, R = −0.8103) and a significant positive corre­
lation with acetic acid (p < 0.01, R = 0.7687) (Figure S3).
3.3.3 Dominant archaeal community
At the genus level, Methanosarcina, Methanobacterium, 
Methanosphaera, Methanothermobacter, and Methano­
brevibacter dominated in the mesophilic digesters 
during the initial stage, with Methanobrevibacter exhibit­
ing the highest RA (Figure 6). In the late stage of diges­
tion, Methanosarcina and Methanobacterium emerged as 
the top two genera in terms of RA. The addition of Air-

in the mesophilic digesters with Air-NBW in this exper­
iment [32,33]. Methanobacterium was significantly posi­
tively correlated with TVFA (p < 0.01, R = 0.6874), 
indicating that it is more tolerant to unfavourable 
environments as a hydrogenotrophic methanogen. 
Methanosphaera utilizes acetic acid as a carbon source 
and hydrogen to reduce methanol, resulting in 
methane yield. An acetic acid-rich environment fosters 
the growth of Methanosphaera, but as acetic acid con­
centrations decline in the later stages of digestion, the 
RA of Methanosphaera correspondingly decreases [38]. 
Methanosphaera exhibited a significant positive corre­
lation with TAN (p < 0.01, R = 0.6552) and UMY (p <  
0.01, R = 0.6656).
Methanosarcina and Methanothermobacter were the 
predominant archaeal genera in the thermophilic diges­
ter on both day 6 and day 28 (Figure 6). The addition of 
NBW enhanced the RA of Methanothermobacter and 
Methanobrevibacter, although their RA declined as diges­
tion progressed. As digestion progressed, the RA of 
Methanosarcina and Methanoculleus increased, with 
NBW addition particularly favouring the rise in RA of 
Methanoculleus during the later stage. Methanosarcina, 
being a mixotrophic methanogen, can utilize acetic 
acid and CO2/H2 for methane yield and is notably toler­
ant to high ammonia concentration [36]. Methanother­
mobacter, Methanobrevibacter, and Methanoculleus are 
hydrogenotrophic methanogens [37,39]. Consequently, 
the addition of NBW effectively promoted the enrich­
ment of hydrogenotrophic methanogens. Among 
them, Methanoculleus 
was considered the most 
effective microorganism at the archaea, which signifi­
cantly impacts methane yield and can tolerate high 
ammonia concentration [39]. Methanoculleus exhibited 
a significant positive correlation with TAN (p < 0.01, R  
= 0.7455) (Figure S3).
4. Conclusion
The addition of NBW enhanced the hydrolysis of CW and 
CM during co-digestion under both thermophilic and 
mesophilic conditions, while also sustaining a stable 
methane yield even at elevated TAN level. Under meso­
philic conditions, methane yields increased by 17.54%, 
8.28%, and 14.72% with the addition of Air-NBW, He- 
NBW, and CO2-NBW, respectively. Similarly, under ther­
mophilic conditions, methane yields increased by 
1.09% and 5.61% with the addition of Air-NBW and N2- 
NBW, respectively. The addition of NBW also enhanced 
microbial abundance and diversity in both mesophilic 
and thermophilic digesters. NBW presents a promising 
alternative to distilled water for AD processes requiring 
dilution; however, further research is needed to eluci­
date the mechanisms through which NBW affects AD 
and 
to 
assess 
the 
impact 
of 
other 
potential 
contaminants.
